To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children who learned of their HIV status at ages 10 to 12 years old were more likely to have viral loads that were undetectable compared to children who learned of the diagnosis younger or older.
children who learn of their HIV status between the ages of 10 and 11 years old are more likely to achieve viral suppression than their peers who learn of their status earlier or later.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between age when children learn of their HIV status and viral load suppression, which is critical for interrupting the transmission of the virus.
how we can best prepare children to live with HIV and achieve suppression.
how we can improve the health of children living with HIV and the health of their communities by improving viral load suppression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal time to inform perinatal infected individuals of their HIV status is when they are 10 to 12 years of age.
the optimal age to disclose a child's HIV status is when the child is 10 to 12 years of age, but this statement is based on the limited data from this study.
children who learned of their HIV status between the age of 10 and 11 were more likely to have a suppressed viral load.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optimal age of disclosure is not yet clear, but it is clear that the age of disclosure matters.
disclosure at an earlier age may not be the most effective way to promote viral suppression in perinatal infected youth.
the optimal time to disclose is between 10 and12 years of age, but that more research is needed to confirm this finding.

age at disclosure does not appear to impact viral load suppression.
